text:
For a typical full-size fridge running through a full day, a **~1,400–2,000 Wh** power station with at least **1,200–1,300 W surge** is a sound target. A **~1,000 Wh** unit covers shorter outages. Check three numbers.

**1. Continuous output (running watts): easy to meet**
A full-size fridge runs at roughly 100–250 W while the compressor is on, so almost any 1,000 W-class station clears this ([BlackBoxSupplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).

**2. Surge output (startup spike): the number that usually decides it**
The compressor can draw about 1,200–2,400 W for a fraction of a second when it starts. If the station's surge rating is lower, its protection can trip at the first start, however much capacity it has ([BlackBoxSupplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage); [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)). Surge figures vary by source and fridge, so check your fridge's label or manual if you can. Also prefer a pure sine wave inverter.

**3. Watt-hours: how long it lasts**
Fridges cycle, so the average draw is much lower than the running watts. One worked example uses a 41 W average (an ENERGY STAR 18 cu ft top-freezer at 362 kWh/year), which gives about 991 Wh per day. After inverter losses and 20% headroom, that's about 1,400 Wh per day ([PowerStations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). To use your own fridge's figure, divide the yellow EnergyGuide label's kWh/year by 8.76 to get average watts.

Runtime estimates differ between sources. One says a ~1,000 Wh unit covers most of a day ([BlackBoxSupplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). Another's model gives about 17 hours for a 1,070 Wh unit ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)). For a 24-hour outage, plan on about 1,400–2,000 Wh. Keep the fridge door shut to save energy.

**Example options**
- **BLUETTI AC200L** (2,048 Wh, 2,400 W continuous, expandable): about $899 list in HomeGridHQ's comparison. You can [buy it from BLUETTI here](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l). That link is an affiliate link, and Dealectric earns a commission if you buy. The page lists a 5% code, AFF5OFF, which it says it tested on 2026-10-21. Checkout is the final word on the price.
- **BLUETTI AC180**: 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W AC, 2,700 W peak, priced about $399–699 ([BlackBoxSupplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). It's a 1,000 Wh-class option for shorter outages. I don't have a direct store link for it, so check the [BlackBoxSupplies guide](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) for current availability.
- **Anker SOLIX S2000** (2,010 Wh, 1,500 W rated, 3,000 W peak): recommended by Anker as a 2 kWh-class refrigerator backup option ([Anker SOLIX](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)). That is the manufacturer's own guide, so weigh it accordingly.

Prices and availability change, so confirm the specs and surge rating on the product page before you buy.
